title: Atlas of Questions
premise: You are assembling a traveling atlas of how people make, challenge and share knowledge. Visit reconstructed workshops and documentary collections, then use their methods on openly speculative future problems. This is a thematic journey, not a claim that history followed one inevitable ladder. Historical people are not simulated speakers; all requests come from fictional curators.

items.label: Observation
items.description: Two otherwise similar pots appear to dry at different rates; the sunnier one seems drier.

items.label: Notebook
items.description: A blank record with spaces for time, conditions and what was actually observed.

items.label: Field note
items.description: The notebook records where, when and how the observation was made. In this teaching case, two pots seem to dry at different rates; a memory of 'the drier one' would lose important context.

items.label: Comparison
items.description: A side-by-side arrangement that makes similarities and differences inspectable.

items.label: Pattern
items.description: Comparing the notes suggests that the sunnier pot dries sooner. A pattern gives us a question, not yet an explanation: the pots might also differ in size.

items.label: Question
items.description: What might explain the difference, and what evidence would distinguish explanations?

items.label: Hypothesis
items.description: One candidate explanation is that greater light exposure increases drying in this setup. It remains a hypothesis rather than a discovery about every plant or climate.

items.label: Prediction
items.description: If light exposure matters here, changing it should change the measured water loss.

items.label: Testable question
items.description: If the proposed explanation matters, otherwise similar pots under different light should lose different amounts of water. That prediction makes a possible failure visible.

items.label: Measuring scale
items.description: A scale whose reading can be checked before trusting a difference between pots.

items.label: Reference standard
items.description: A known reference used to detect an offset in the measuring device.

items.label: Calibrated scale
items.description: A known reference exposes an offset in the scale. Calibration ties readings to a standard; it does not remove every source of error.

items.label: Repeated readings
items.description: Several measurements made under recorded conditions, including their fluctuations.

items.label: Measurement series
items.description: Repeated readings reveal small fluctuations that a single reading would hide. Keep the variation rather than choosing the most pleasing number.

items.label: Measurement record
items.description: The record pairs each reading with its conditions. Another observer can now ask whether the difference is larger than the measurement uncertainty.

items.label: Variable
items.description: A quantity that can take different values; in the opening experiment it is light exposure.

items.label: Fixed conditions
items.description: The teaching setup holds pot size and starting water constant while changing light.

items.label: Controlled comparison
items.description: The teaching comparison changes light while holding pot size and starting water fixed. Controlling these conditions narrows the explanations; it does not guarantee all confounders vanished.

items.label: Experimental protocol
items.description: The written protocol says what will be compared, measured and recorded. It turns a private trick into a procedure another person can attempt.

items.label: Repeatable experiment
items.description: The arrangement can be repeated from the record. A later attempt may disagree: repeatability is an opportunity to test the result, not a promise of agreement.

items.label: Claim
items.description: The speaker says equal payments make the proposed levy fair.

items.label: Reason
items.description: Everyone pays the same numerical amount: this is the speaker's offered justification.

items.label: Argument
items.description: The speaker claims the new levy is fair because everyone pays the same amount. A reason is now visible, so an audience can challenge its relevance instead of merely disliking the conclusion.

items.label: Stated assumptions
items.description: The proposed argument assumes equal amounts also impose equal burdens.

items.label: Explicit premises
items.description: The hidden premise is that equal amounts imply equal burdens. Naming it reveals where people who agree about the figures may still disagree.

items.label: Inference rule
items.description: A supplied valid argument pattern to compare with this particular set of premises.

items.label: Valid argument
items.description: In this supplied example, 'all citizens covered by rule R must pay; this person is covered by R; therefore this person must pay' has a valid form. Validity does not establish that the rule or premises are just or true.

items.label: General claim
items.description: Every equal payment imposes an equal burden: a claim vulnerable to one counterexample.

items.label: Contrary case
items.description: Two households have very different incomes but must pay the same amount.

items.label: Counterexample
items.description: One low-income household and one wealthy household can pay the same amount while bearing very different burdens. That counterexample defeats the universal equal-burden claim, not every possible argument for the levy.

items.label: Word
items.description: The contested word is 'equal'; the debate uses it in more than one sense.

items.label: Competing meanings
items.description: Equal amount and equal sacrifice are different possible meanings in this argument.

items.label: Ambiguity
items.description: The speakers have used 'equal' to mean both equal amounts and equal sacrifice. A shared word was concealing two different questions.

items.label: Context
items.description: The surrounding passage or situation helps identify which meaning a speaker intended.

items.label: Disambiguated term
items.description: Here 'equal amount' refers only to the numerical payment. The clarified term prevents one meaning being silently substituted for another.

items.label: Precise question
items.description: The question becomes 'Which principle of fairness should determine the payment?' Clear wording exposes a genuine disagreement rather than automatically resolving it.

items.label: Manuscript copy
items.description: One witness to a passage, with its own spelling, omissions and corrections.

items.label: Variant manuscript
items.description: Another witness preserves a different word at the disputed passage.

items.label: Collation
items.description: The copies preserve different words in the same passage. Collation puts the alternatives beside one another without deciding that the oldest-looking copy must be right.

items.label: Passage lemma
items.description: A short quotation identifies the passage under discussion, without modern line numbering.

items.label: Variant table
items.description: A quoted opening phrase—the lemma—identifies the passage being discussed. This reconstruction does not give ancient Alexandrian commentary modern line numbers.

items.label: Scribal patterns
items.description: Shared omissions and repeated copying mistakes can suggest relationships, but not a certain family tree.

items.label: Textual family
items.description: Shared copying errors suggest relationships between these copies. This is the modern curator's tentative family reconstruction; borrowing between copies can defeat a simple tree.

items.label: Damaged passage
items.description: Part of the text is missing; restoration must be distinguished from surviving words.

items.label: Reconstructed reading
items.description: The missing reading is proposed from the surviving variants and copying patterns. It remains a reconstruction, not recovered certainty, and is visibly marked as such.

items.label: Uncertainty marks
items.description: Visible signs distinguish conjectural restorations from securely readable text.

items.label: Critical text
items.description: The editor distinguishes readable text from conjecture. A small uncertainty mark prevents the restoration from masquerading as an untouched ancient witness.

items.label: Critical edition
items.description: The text is accompanied by alternatives and explanations. Readers can inspect the editorial judgment rather than being asked to trust a silently repaired passage.

items.label: Foreign passage
items.description: A passage containing a word with more than one plausible translation.

items.label: Bilingual glossary
items.description: Candidate correspondences between languages, useful but insufficient without context.

items.label: Draft translation
items.description: The first translation chooses one meaning for an ambiguous word. Its fluency is useful, but does not prove it preserved every implication of the source.

items.label: Annotated translation
items.description: A note explains the rejected meaning and why the context favored this one. The translation now exposes an interpretive decision instead of hiding it.

items.label: Parallel edition
items.description: Source text and translation can be compared passage by passage. The parallel edition gives readers a way to disagree with the translator.

items.label: Quantity
items.description: The amount owed in the workshop's illustrative transaction.

items.label: Place value
items.description: The value of a digit depends on its position;30 and3 use the same digit differently.

items.label: Numeral
items.description: The position of a digit changes its value: in a decimal notation, 3 in 30 is not 3 in 3. This modern demonstration makes place value explicit; it is not an exclusive origin claim.

items.label: Counting board
items.description: A physical aid for keeping track of intermediate quantities in a calculation.

items.label: Written calculation
items.description: The written calculation keeps intermediate quantities outside the calculator's memory. Another person can retrace the arithmetic and locate an error.

items.label: Transaction record
items.description: A dated record of what was received, paid or remains owed.

items.label: Ledger
items.description: Transactions are recorded as amounts owed and received. A running account reveals an unpaid balance that isolated receipts can conceal.

items.label: Opposing entries
items.description: Entries that should reconcile if this example account has been recorded consistently.

items.label: Balanced ledger
items.description: The example's opposing entries reconcile to the same total. This is a balanced account, not proof that every transaction was legitimate.

items.label: Unknown quantity
items.description: The unknown x in the teaching problem x + 5 = 12.

items.label: Equality
items.description: A statement that two expressions have the same value in the problem.

items.label: Equation
items.description: A workshop problem becomes x + 5 = 12: the unknown is represented without guessing its value. The equality states a constraint, not a magic answer.

items.label: Equal operations
items.description: Apply the same permitted operation to both sides to preserve this equality.

items.label: Equivalent equation
items.description: Subtracting 5 from both sides preserves this equality, leaving x = 7. Applying an operation on only one side would change the problem.

items.label: Inverse operation
items.description: Subtract5 to undo adding5 in the supplied linear equation; not a universal equation solver.

items.label: Solved equation
items.description: The value 7 satisfies the original equation when substituted back. This recipe solves the supplied linear case, not every possible equation by one inverse operation.

items.label: General solution
items.description: The same reasoning gives x = b − a for x + a = b. One worked transaction has become a reusable method.

items.label: Square diagram
items.description: A square-and-strips drawing representing x² + 6x in the modern teaching example.

items.label: Missing corner
items.description: The3-by-3 corner of area9 that completes the square in that example.

items.label: Completing the square
items.description: For x² + 6x, adding a square of area9 completes the larger square (x + 3)². The geometry explains why a correction term must be added, not merely memorized.

items.label: Quadratic method
items.description: Completing the square turns a quadratic into a form from which candidate roots can be checked. The algebraic method extends the geometric example; domain and sign conditions still matter.

items.label: Light source
items.description: A source whose position can be changed to test where light reaches the screen.

items.label: Straight path
items.description: A proposed straight light path in a uniform medium, before refraction is introduced.

items.label: Light ray
items.description: A ray represents a possible path of light, not a physical thread. Moving the source changes which paths reach the screen.

items.label: Opaque barrier
items.description: A shape that blocks light rather than transmitting it.

items.label: Shadow
items.description: The barrier blocks some paths from the source, leaving a shadow. Its outline changes when source, barrier or screen moves, so the shadow alone does not uniquely reveal the object.

items.label: Small aperture
items.description: A small opening that selects a narrow bundle of paths through a barrier.

items.label: Narrow beam
items.description: The small aperture admits a narrow bundle of paths. It helps separate where light comes from instead of flooding the whole screen.

items.label: Screen
items.description: A surface on which arriving light can be observed.

items.label: Projected spot
items.description: The spot marks where the admitted light reaches the screen. Changing the aperture's position gives an observable test of the path model.

items.label: Scene
items.description: A courtyard with distinguishable upper and lower features, used to test image inversion.

items.label: Inverted image
items.description: In the dark room, rays from the top and bottom of the scene cross at the aperture and make an inverted image. Stray light would make that image harder to see.

items.label: Enclosure plan
items.description: A plan for excluding stray light around an aperture and screen.

items.label: Camera obscura
items.description: An enclosure and small opening make a portable camera obscura. This teaching construction turns a room-sized optical effect into a usable reference tool.

items.label: Curved glass
items.description: A simplified lens element whose shape can redirect light toward an image.

items.label: Refraction model
items.description: At a boundary between materials, light can change direction. The simplified ray model predicts a bent path; it omits the full angle-dependent calculation.

items.label: Focused image
items.description: A suitably arranged lens brings rays from a scene point toward a corresponding image point. Moving the screen away from that position blurs the image.

items.label: Optical experiment
items.description: The aperture, source and screen can be varied and the observations repeated. The resulting evidence bears on an account of vision, not on every aspect of human perception at once.

items.label: Image-forming model
items.description: The model connects scene points, light paths and image points. It explains the inversion without needing a picture to travel intact through the hole.

items.label: Picture plane
items.description: The imaginary flat surface onto which the chosen view is projected.

items.label: Projection construction
items.description: In this modern teaching reconstruction, the optical model supplies a chosen viewpoint and picture plane. It does not claim that Renaissance perspective historically required a camera obscura.

items.label: Parallel lines
items.description: Courtyard edges that are parallel in the represented space and recede from the viewer.

items.label: Vanishing point
items.description: A family of parallel lines receding from the picture plane converges toward one vanishing point in this construction. Different directions need not share that point.

items.label: Horizon
items.description: The eye-level reference in this one-viewpoint construction.

items.label: Perspective grid
items.description: The horizon and vanishing point organize a grid of receding space. The grid is a particular viewing convention, not a ranking of artistic traditions.

items.label: Courtyard plan
items.description: A plan showing the courtyard's walls, columns and relative positions.

items.label: Perspective drawing
items.description: The courtyard plan is projected from one selected viewpoint. Change that viewpoint and a different drawing can be equally coherent.

items.label: Measured proportions
items.description: Recorded ratios from the courtyard plan, used to check the projected drawing.

items.label: Scaled architectural view
items.description: Measured proportions connect the image to the courtyard plan. The view is now checkable, while still omitting parts hidden from its chosen observer.

items.label: Pigment
items.description: A coloring material; it needs a medium to become usable paint.

items.label: Binder
items.description: A medium that holds pigment together and attaches it to the surface.

items.label: Paint
items.description: Pigment supplies color and a binder holds it to the surface. Different combinations permit different marks; paint is not simply colored light.

items.label: Light study
items.description: Notes on the courtyard's broad illuminated and shaded areas.

items.label: Observational sketch
items.description: The camera obscura supplies a reference for the courtyard's contours and light. The artist can still simplify or depart from it deliberately.

items.label: Tonal study
items.description: Broad light and dark masses make the courtyard legible before detail. This tonal study can support depth even without a precise geometric grid.

items.label: Spatial painting
items.description: Tonal relationships and perspective now cooperate in the painting. Neither method alone determines what the viewer should care about.

items.label: Foreground form
items.description: A nearby column that hides part of the background wall.

items.label: Background form
items.description: A wall partly hidden by the foreground column.

items.label: Occlusion study
items.description: A foreground column hides part of the wall behind it. Occlusion supplies a depth cue without requiring the viewer to calculate a vanishing point.

items.label: Courtyard painting
items.description: The courtyard has a coherent spatial reading assembled from projection, tone and overlap. The achievement is one convincing image, not a universal solution to painting.

items.label: Anatomical observation
items.description: A recorded adult-human jaw observation, explicitly distinguished from infant development and other species.

items.label: Anatomy record
items.description: The teaching record distinguishes the adult human lower jaw from the inherited two-part account. Age and specimen identity are recorded: adult fusion cannot be generalized to every developmental stage.

items.label: Drawing
items.description: An inspectable anatomical sketch rather than a claim resting solely on the observer's memory.

items.label: Anatomical plate
items.description: The drawing makes the observed jaw contour inspectable away from the specimen. A plate is an argument made visible, and can introduce its own distortions.

items.label: Labels
items.description: Names attached to particular observed structures so disagreement can be located precisely.

items.label: Labeled anatomy
items.description: Labels connect claims to particular structures instead of to an undifferentiated picture. Readers can now point to exactly where an account disagrees.

items.label: Sequence
items.description: An ordering of records or diagrams that makes before-and-after comparisons possible.

items.label: Anatomical atlas
items.description: The plates are organized for comparison. An atlas makes repeated inspection possible; its authority still depends on the observations and drawing choices behind it.

items.label: Inherited diagram
items.description: The teaching collection includes the older two-part jaw account alongside the later adult-human observation.

items.label: Anatomical discrepancy
items.description: The inherited two-part lower-jaw account and the adult human observation do not match. This specific discrepancy is more useful than declaring all older medicine mistaken.

items.label: Species comparison
items.description: Separate records identify which observations concern humans and which concern other animals.

items.label: Comparative anatomy
items.description: Comparing species and specimen ages asks whether an animal-based account was transferred too broadly. A difference must be located before it can support a correction.

items.label: Repeated observation
items.description: Additional independently recorded specimens test whether the claimed discrepancy persists.

items.label: Supported correction
items.description: Repeated adult-human observations support the correction in this bounded case. The historical research contrasts Vesalius's earlier Tabulae with the Fabrica; his own account changed too.

items.label: Source attribution
items.description: A record of who made a claim, which work contains it and which observation is being cited.

items.label: Annotated correction
items.description: The note identifies the claim, observations and remaining limits. Correcting the jaw account does not erase Vesalius's continuing debts to Galen or certify every claim in the atlas.

items.label: Heart rate
items.description: Illustrative teaching rate:60 beats per minute. This is not asserted to be Harvey's own chosen number.

items.label: Stroke volume estimate
items.description: Illustrative teaching estimate:50mL per beat, used with an explicitly stated heart rate.

items.label: Flow estimate
items.description: This illustrative modern calculation uses a heart rate of60 beats/minute and a stroke-volume estimate of50mL/beat: flow is3L/minute. These are teaching numbers, not a quotation of Harvey's estimates.

items.label: Time interval
items.description: The measured elapsed time; each worked example states its duration and units.

items.label: Throughput estimate
items.description: At the illustrative flow of3L/minute, ten minutes gives30L passing through. Keeping units visible prevents multiplying a heartbeat count by time twice.

items.label: Body volume estimate
items.description: Illustrative standing blood volume:5L, for comparison with throughput rather than clinical advice.

items.label: Quantity contradiction
items.description: Thirty liters passing through in ten minutes greatly exceeds an illustrative5L blood volume. A simple one-pass consumption account would require implausibly rapid replacement; recirculation is a candidate explanation.

items.label: Valve drawing
items.description: A recorded diagram of a vein valve whose orientation suggests a permitted direction of flow.

items.label: Direction test
items.description: Historical observation notes comparing the directions in which a vein can be emptied and refilled.

items.label: One-way valve model
items.description: The supplied vein observations show flow favored in one direction. A valve can constrain movement without itself being the pump.

items.label: Vessel diagram
items.description: A map of connected vessels, initially without a complete directional account.

items.label: Directional vessel map
items.description: The vessel diagram records those directions rather than merely drawing connected tubes. It narrows which possible circulation routes fit the observations.

items.label: Heart diagram
items.description: A schematic pumping heart, offered as part of a candidate circuit.

items.label: Circulation model
items.description: The heart and directed vessels form a candidate circuit. The diagram predicts a return route; drawing it is not yet observing every connection.

items.label: Recirculation argument
items.description: The circuit explains how a large throughput can coexist with a much smaller standing blood volume. This is one part of Harvey's reasoning, not a replacement for his other arguments.

items.label: Recorded intervention
items.description: Historical experimental observations to compare with the circulation model's predictions; no procedure is prescribed.

items.label: Tested circulation account
items.description: Recorded interventions are compared with the circuit's predictions. Agreement strengthens this account, while the archive preserves that quantitative, experimental and analogical arguments worked together.

items.label: Microscope drawing
items.description: A later microscopic tissue drawing, separated in date and attribution from Harvey's work.

items.label: Fine vessel observation
items.description: Malpighi's later evidence of fine connections in frog tissue, reported in1661.

items.label: Capillary evidence
items.caveat: Malpighi’s later observations, not Harvey’s own microscope evidence.
items.description: Malpighi's later microscopic observations, reported in1661, showed fine connections in frog tissue. These are not observations made by Harvey himself.

items.label: Connected circulation diagram
items.description: The later capillary evidence supplies an observed connection that the earlier circuit needed. The combined diagram spans different investigators and generations.

items.label: Position model
items.description: A smooth fitted position function and its underlying recorded positions; the distinction from raw samples is retained.

items.label: Average velocity
items.description: In this modern model an object moves from0m to6m in3s, giving average velocity +2m/s. Direction is part of velocity; a distance alone would omit it.

items.label: Shrinking interval
items.description: A sequence of smaller time intervals used to ask whether average slopes approach a limit.

items.label: Instantaneous velocity
items.description: For a smooth fitted position model, slopes over shrinking intervals approach an instantaneous velocity. Real sampled observations require a model and retain measurement uncertainty.

items.label: Velocity change
items.description: In the example velocity changes from2m/s to8m/s over3s.

items.label: Average acceleration
items.description: A velocity change from2m/s to8m/s over3s gives average acceleration2m/s². This finite-interval result is not automatically instantaneous acceleration throughout the interval.

items.label: Curve
items.description: A drawn mathematical function; smoothness is a property to check, not assume everywhere.

items.label: Secant line
items.description: A line joining two nearby points on the curve, giving an average slope.

items.label: Difference quotient
items.description: A secant slope compares a curve's change in value with its change in input. Shrinking the interval asks whether those slopes approach a stable limit.

items.label: Limit
items.description: The proposed value approached as an interval shrinks; it need not exist for every function.

items.label: Derivative
items.description: Where the limit exists, the derivative describes local change. A sharp corner is a useful warning: not every drawn curve has a derivative everywhere.

items.label: Velocity function
items.description: Differentiating the smooth position model produces its velocity function. This is a result about the fitted model, not direct differentiation of isolated raw measurements.

items.label: Small time slices
items.description: Short intervals used to sum signed velocity×time contributions.

items.label: Displacement sum
items.description: Small signed velocity×time contributions add to displacement. Traveling +6m then−4m gives net displacement2m, even though the total distance traveled is10m.

items.label: Integral
items.description: The integral is the limit of these displacement sums. To obtain total distance, integrate speed—the absolute value of velocity—instead; the distinction survives arbitrarily fine slices.

items.label: Mass
items.description: The mass used with acceleration in the idealized Newtonian force requirement.

items.label: Force model
items.description: Mass times the example’s average acceleration gives its average net-force requirement in the Newtonian model. It does not by itself identify which physical interaction supplies that force.

items.label: Orbital model
items.description: A proposed inverse-square attraction is tested against the motion requirements and recorded orbits in this idealized Newtonian case. The candidate law supplies content that 'force' alone could not.

items.label: Possible outcomes
items.description: Winner sequences AA, AB, BA and BB for the next two rounds of the fair game.

items.label: Equal likelihood
items.description: An explicit assumption of fair independent rounds in this example, not a property of every outcome list.

items.label: Equiprobable outcome list
items.description: The next two fair rounds have four equally likely winner sequences: AA, AB, BA, BB. If the match finishes early, the unused round can still be listed to compare equally likely cases.

items.label: Favorable outcomes
items.description: The sequences in which the current2–1 leader eventually wins the first-to-three match.

items.label: Probability
items.description: In this equiprobable example, favorable cases divided by all cases gives a probability. A general sample space need not have equal probabilities; that assumption belongs to this game.

items.label: Payout
items.description: The amount assigned to each final outcome when calculating an expected value.

items.label: Expected value
items.description: Weight each payout by its probability and add. Expected value describes an average under the model, not what any one play must pay.

items.label: Unfinished game
items.description: A fair first-to-three match stops at2–1 with a four-coin stake to divide.

items.label: Fair stake division
items.description: At2–1 in a first-to-three match, the leader wins unless the other player wins twice: probability3/4. Divide four coins as3 and1, not in the current-score ratio2:1.

items.label: Repeated trials
items.description: Recorded repetitions that can test how well an assumed chance model fits observed outcomes.

items.label: Outcome counts
items.description: The number of occurrences of each recorded outcome, including inconvenient results.

items.label: Frequency table
items.description: The frequency table records repeated outcomes, including disappointing runs. A short sequence need not resemble its long-run model closely.

items.label: Empirical distribution
items.description: Relative frequencies form an empirical distribution of this record. The record can challenge an assumed model without proving exactly what will happen next.

items.label: Loss amounts
items.description: Consequences attached to possible outcomes; the same probability can matter differently for different losses.

items.label: Risk table
items.description: The risk table keeps losses beside their probabilities. Equal expected values can conceal very different worst cases and matter differently to different players.

items.label: Conditional event
items.description: An observed event that narrows which outcomes remain under consideration.

items.label: Conditional probability
items.description: Conditioning restricts attention to cases compatible with the observed event. P(A given B) need not equal P(B given A); reversing them can change an argument completely.

items.label: Likelihood ratio
items.description: Modern extension: the evidence is three times as probable under one specified hypothesis as under its alternative.

items.label: Prior odds
items.description: Modern extension: initial odds1:4 for those two hypotheses, before the stated evidence.

items.label: Updated odds
items.description: This explicitly modern extension multiplies prior odds by a likelihood ratio. Prior odds1:4 and likelihood ratio3 give posterior odds3:4—not probability3/4, and not a result from the1654 letters.

items.label: Revised risk estimate
items.description: The revised probabilities change the risk estimate while leaving the possible losses visible. The likelihood model and prior remain contestable; a numerical update is not manufactured certainty.

items.label: Oscillator
items.description: A repeating motion intended to supply a timekeeping reference.

items.label: Escapement
items.description: The mechanism that meters the clock movement in relation to the oscillator.

items.label: Clock movement
items.description: The oscillator supplies a repeated motion and the escapement meters the clock's movement. A regular tick on land is only the beginning of the navigation problem.

items.label: Temperature compensation
items.description: A proposed adjustment to reduce changes in rate with temperature; its effectiveness must be tested.

items.label: Compensated clock
items.description: Temperature compensation aims to reduce changes in timekeeping as conditions vary. The design must be tested; attaching the name 'compensation' does not establish its accuracy.

items.label: Motion-resistant mounting
items.description: A design intended to keep the timekeeper operating through ship motion.

items.label: Marine timekeeper
items.description: The mounting is intended to keep time through ship motion. Sea conditions ask a different question from a quiet workshop demonstration.

items.label: Sea trial log
items.description: A record of timekeeper behavior during an actual or reconstructed sea trial, not merely a bench demonstration.

items.label: Tested chronometer
items.description: The trial log records how the timekeeper performed at sea. One good voyage still leaves durability, cost and repeatable manufacture open to examination.

items.label: Local noon
items.description: The ship's observed noon; the reference-clock reading must be taken at this same instant.

items.label: Reference time
items.description: The idealized example's reference clock reads14:00 at the instant of local noon.

items.label: Time difference
items.description: At the instant of local noon, this idealized example's reference clock reads14:00. The simultaneous difference is two hours; comparing readings from different moments would be meaningless.

items.label: Earth rotation rate
items.description: The idealized conversion uses15degrees of rotation per hour.

items.label: Longitude estimate
items.description: Earth turns15degrees per hour, so that two-hour difference corresponds to30degrees. With the reference clock ahead at local noon, this idealized position is west of the reference meridian.

items.label: Chronometer fix
items.description: The tested timekeeper supports this clock-based fix, with its accumulated error carried forward. A reliable instrument and a correct calculation are distinct requirements.

items.label: Corrected Moon–star angle
items.description: An idealized angular observation after necessary corrections; the game does not teach the complete reduction procedure.

items.label: Lunar tables
items.description: Tables connecting the Moon's apparent position with reference time, with their own uncertainties.

items.label: Reference sky time
items.description: The corrected Moon–star observation is compared with lunar tables to estimate reference time. This idealized card assumes necessary observational corrections; it is not a complete navigation procedure.

items.label: Lunar-distance fix
items.description: Reference sky time is compared with the ship's local astronomical time at that same observation. Local noon from another moment is not a substitute.

items.label: Cross-checked position
items.description: In the fictional trial, clock and lunar fixes differ by2degrees. The disagreement triggers checking errors before approaching a coast; averaging them blindly could preserve a shared mistake.

items.label: Sediment
items.description: Material accumulated in the section's earlier depositional episode.

items.label: Layer diagram
items.description: The observed order and orientation of the lower and upper beds.

items.label: Sedimentary sequence
items.description: The lower and upper beds record separate episodes of sediment accumulation. Their order is evidence; the section does not supply a calendar date by itself.

items.label: Tilted bedding
items.description: Older beds now stand at a steep angle beneath differently oriented younger beds.

items.label: Deformation record
items.description: The older beds are now steeply tilted. Their present orientation records deformation after deposition rather than proving sediment originally fell vertically.

items.label: Eroded surface
items.description: A boundary that truncates the older beds and indicates missing material.

items.label: Erosion interval
items.description: The tilted beds are truncated at a surface. Material is missing: erosion can leave a boundary that is positive evidence of an intervening event.

items.label: Younger strata
items.description: Later beds laid across the truncated, tilted older sequence.

items.label: Unconformity
items.description: Younger beds lie across the eroded older beds at a different angle. The angular unconformity requires more than one uninterrupted episode of deposition.

items.label: Stratigraphic section
items.description: The labeled section keeps the crossing relationships visible: deposition, deformation, erosion, then renewed deposition. A drawing makes the proposed event order checkable.

items.label: Relative chronology
items.description: The crossing relationships constrain a relative chronology. They establish before and after without assigning an unsupported number of years.

items.label: Slow process observation
items.description: Evidence that ordinary deposition and erosion can act repeatedly over long durations.

items.label: Deep-time argument
items.description: Repeated ordinary processes require substantial time in Hutton's account. Siccar Point supports that reasoning; it did not create the whole theory in a single instant.

items.label: Fossil assemblage
items.description: A later Smith-style comparison of characteristic fossils associated with particular strata.

items.label: Correlated strata
items.description: A later comparison introduces William Smith's use of characteristic fossil assemblages to recognize strata. This is not attributed to Hutton's1788 visit.

items.label: Distant section
items.description: Another measured sequence used to test whether fossil-bearing layers can be correlated across the region.

items.label: Regional sequence
items.description: Comparing fossil-bearing sections can connect layers across a region even where surface appearance differs. Smith's1815 mapping is the historical case; any particular match still needs evidence.

items.label: Geological history
items.description: The account distinguishes Hutton's event sequence from the later fossil-mapping comparison. The atlas now explains both missing time in one section and correlations between sections.

items.label: Population
items.description: A group of organisms whose recorded characteristics vary among individuals.

items.label: Variation record
items.description: Observed differences within the population, not just differences between named species.

items.label: Variable population
items.description: The recorded population contains differences among individuals. Treating every specimen as an imperfect copy of one ideal would discard the variation the explanation needs.

items.label: Heritable differences
items.description: Differences that recur across generations in the teaching example.

items.label: Heritable variation
items.description: Some recorded differences recur across generations in the teaching case. Heritability, not merely visible difference, is needed for this selection model.

items.label: Unequal reproduction
items.description: Recorded differences in descendants left under the specified conditions.

items.label: Selection model
items.description: Individuals with a heritable difference leave different numbers of descendants under these conditions. That can change a population without any individual deciding to evolve.

items.label: Changing environment
items.description: A change that may alter which traits help or hinder reproduction.

items.label: Adaptation model
items.description: A trait helpful in one environment can be costly in another. Adaptation here is a context-dependent fit, not movement toward a universal best organism.

items.label: Related forms
items.description: Specimens offered for a tentative relationship comparison.

items.label: Shared characters
items.description: Similar features that might indicate common ancestry or independent convergence.

items.label: Relationship hypothesis
items.description: Shared characters suggest a relationship hypothesis. Similarity can also arise independently, so resemblance alone is not an infallible family tree.

items.label: Divergence
items.description: Differences accumulating between lineages in the proposed historical model.

items.label: Branching descent
items.description: The branching diagram represents divergence, not a ladder with humans at its summit. Living branches have their own histories rather than being unfinished ancestors of one another.

items.label: Island species
items.description: A collection whose geographic distribution demands explanation, not a ladder ranking its inhabitants.

items.label: Geographic barriers
items.description: Features that can reduce exchange between populations without predetermining their evolutionary outcomes.

items.label: Isolation hypothesis
items.description: A geographic barrier can reduce exchange between populations. It proposes a mechanism for divergence, but isolation alone does not determine the eventual outcome.

items.label: Biogeographic account
items.description: The island distribution is compared with a branching account and barriers. Geography becomes evidence about relationships rather than decoration around a list of species.

items.label: Fossil sequence
items.description: Earlier forms preserved unevenly through time; an incomplete historical record.

items.label: Historical descent evidence
items.description: The fossil sequence tests whether the proposed history fits earlier forms. Incomplete preservation limits what absence can establish.

items.label: Evolutionary explanation
items.description: The explanation joins branching history with a possible mechanism of change. Darwin and Wallace are contributors to this case, not licenses to turn biological selection into a moral rule.

items.label: Death register
items.description: Recorded deaths with addresses and dates, subject to the limitations of historical reporting.

items.label: Street plan
items.description: A map for locating recorded cases, without automatically supplying population denominators.

items.label: Case map
items.description: The marks locate recorded deaths; Snow’s historical map used bars. A dense cluster can reflect exposure, population density or reporting, so a map is a question-generating tool rather than a verdict.

items.label: Household counts
items.description: Numbers of households served, needed to compare rates rather than raw death totals.

items.label: Mortality rates
items.description: Deaths are compared with households served. A supplier with more deaths but many more customers need not have the higher rate.

items.label: Water supplier records
items.description: Records used to identify which company supplied particular households.

items.label: Supplier comparison
items.description: Rates are grouped by water supplier rather than just by street. The comparison now addresses a possible exposure difference.

items.label: Intermingled households
items.description: Nearby houses served by different suppliers, allowing a bounded comparison within shared neighborhoods.

items.label: Natural-experiment comparison
items.description: Intermingled households help compare suppliers within shared neighborhoods. This was not random assignment; remaining household differences still deserve investigation.

items.label: Interview record
items.description: A resident reports a water source different from the one expected at the address.

items.label: Exposure history
items.description: A witness reports using a different water source from the one expected at the address. Interview evidence exposes a possible classification error in the neat map.

items.label: Exposure classification
items.description: Receipts and supplier records are checked against the household account. Exposure must be established, not guessed solely from geographic proximity.

items.label: Exposure-risk estimate
items.description: The revised exposure groups change the calculated risk comparison. A quantitative result depends on how cases and denominators were classified.

items.label: Converging evidence
items.description: The map, interviews and rate comparison address related parts of the same question. They overlap in data and are not automatically independent confirmations.

items.label: Alternative explanations
items.description: Other differences between households that might contribute to the observed rates.

items.label: Causal assessment
items.description: Alternative explanations are weighed against the exposure evidence. This supports a causal assessment while retaining observational limitations.

items.label: Feasible intervention
items.description: A proposed way to reduce hazardous water exposure while uncertainty is still being assessed.

items.label: Water-safety recommendation
items.description: A water-safety intervention can be recommended without pretending every causal uncertainty disappeared. The archive does not claim that removing one pump handle alone ended the outbreak.

items.label: Light-sensitive paper
items.description: A historical photographic material represented without a preparation recipe.

items.label: Latent paper image
items.description: The light-sensitive paper records exposure before a clearly visible image appears. This historical-process model describes an effect, not a chemical preparation recipe.

items.label: Development process
items.description: A historical processing step represented by its effect on a latent paper image.

items.label: Visible paper negative
items.description: Development makes the paper negative visible. Light and dark are reversed, which will matter when another image is made from it.

items.label: Fixing process
items.description: The modeled step that stabilizes the image for further use; not a guarantee of indefinite preservation.

items.label: Stable negative
items.description: Fixing makes the negative sufficiently stable for the historical workflow. Preservation still depends on materials and conditions; 'stable' does not mean eternal.

items.label: Contact printing
items.description: Making a positive impression with a negative in contact with another light-sensitive surface.

items.label: Positive print
items.description: Contact printing from the negative produces a positive image. One preserved negative makes repeat copies possible, unlike a unique direct-positive object.

items.label: Scale marker
items.description: A reference of known size visible in the photographed plane.

items.label: Measured photograph
items.description: A scale marker gives the photograph a reference for size in its plane. Perspective and camera position still limit measurements elsewhere in the scene.

items.label: Time series
items.description: Images or readings with recorded times, allowing changes to be compared.

items.label: Photographic record
items.description: Images taken at recorded times reveal change that a single photograph cannot. Differences in lighting or camera position can also masquerade as change.

items.label: Context annotation
items.description: Notes about provenance, conditions and interpretation that travel with the evidence.

items.label: Annotated visual archive
items.description: Context records explain when, where and why the images were made. A photograph can be evidence without being an interpretation-free window onto the past.

items.label: Reproduction sequence
items.description: A documented way to produce several prints from the preserved negative.

items.label: Print edition
items.description: Several prints can be made from the negative and compared by different viewers. Reproducibility changes who can inspect an image, not whether every interpretation is correct.

items.label: Alphabet
items.description: The teaching communication example has two symbols, represented by0 and1.

items.label: Symbol assignment
items.description: Sender and receiver agree which physical signal represents each symbol.

items.label: Codebook
items.description: The teaching codebook assigns0 and1 to two signals. Sender and receiver must share the assignment before a pattern can carry the intended message.

items.label: Message
items.description: The example message contains the intended bit0; its semantic truth is a separate question.

items.label: Encoded message
items.description: The intended bit0 is encoded for transmission. Meaning is agreed outside the symbol itself; a code can transmit a false statement perfectly.

items.label: Noise record
items.description: The demonstration channel flips at most one bit per three-bit group.

items.label: Corrupted transmission
items.description: The teaching channel flips at most one bit in each three-bit group. This explicit error budget defines what the later correction demonstration can promise.

items.label: Redundant symbols
items.description: The specified repetition code uses000 for0 and111 for1.

items.label: Error-detecting code
items.description: Repeating0 as000 and1 as111 makes a one-bit discrepancy detectable. Merely adding unspecified redundancy would not provide the same guarantee.

items.label: Correction rule
items.description: Majority decoding for the stated repetition code and one-error-per-group bound.

items.label: Error-correcting code
items.description: Majority decoding corrects one flipped bit in these three-bit groups. Two flipped bits can defeat it; an arbitrary detection code cannot correct arbitrary errors.

items.label: Recoverable message
items.description: Under the stated one-error-per-group bound, the receiver recovers the sent bit. The guarantee belongs to the model and bound, not to every noisy channel.

items.label: Pair frequencies
items.description: Compression example: source-bit pairs00,01,10,11 have probabilities0.7,0.1,0.1,0.1; these are paired-block frequencies, not a claim of independent individual bits.

items.label: Information measure
items.description: For compression we now group source bits into pairs:00,01,10,11 have supplied probabilities0.7,0.1,0.1,0.1. These four block outcomes—not single binary symbols—have unequal frequencies. Their uncertainty measure still says nothing about truth or wisdom.

items.label: Efficient code
items.description: Encode source pairs00→0,01→10,10→110,11→111. No codeword starts another, so concatenated codewords remain decodable. The common00 pair gets one bit; rarer pairs cost two or three. The earlier single-bit repetition example is unchanged.

items.label: Channel constraint
items.description: A limited transmission capacity; compression gains and error-control overhead compete for it.

items.label: Compression scheme
items.description: Expected length is0.7×1 +0.1×2 +0.1×3 +0.1×3 =1.5 bits per source pair, versus2 bits without compression. This model gives a25% average reduction before error-control overhead, not a shorter encoding for every pair.

items.label: Reliable communication scheme
items.description: Compression and error control address different pressures: saving capacity and surviving noise. The scheme makes their assumptions explicit rather than promising perfect communication at no cost.

items.label: Variation estimate
items.description: A summary of spread among repeated readings, distinct from systematic bias.

items.label: Error bars
items.description: Repeated readings vary around an estimate. The error bars state the chosen uncertainty summary; their meaning must be named rather than inferred from their appearance.

items.label: Sample size
items.description: The number of observations contributing to an estimate, not a substitute for a suitable sampling process.

items.label: Precision estimate
items.description: More observations can sharpen an estimate under the stated sampling model. Repeating a biased procedure more often does not remove its bias.

items.label: Sampling plan
items.description: A record of how cases were selected and which population the estimate is intended to describe.

items.label: Uncertainty statement
items.description: The uncertainty statement records sampling assumptions as well as a number. Precision about the wrong population can still mislead.

items.label: Rival model
items.description: An alternative account that predicts a different result for the proposed new observation.

items.label: Model comparison
items.description: Two models make different predictions for a new observation. A comparison becomes informative when evidence could favor one over the other.

items.label: New observations
items.description: Evidence collected after the competing predictions were recorded.

items.label: Predictive test
items.description: The new observation is compared with predictions written beforehand. A model modified after seeing the result has not passed the same test.

items.label: Held-out observations
items.description: Cases withheld from fitting, retained for a separate performance assessment.

items.label: Out-of-sample assessment
items.description: Held-out observations test performance beyond the fitted examples. Repeatedly choosing models on the held-out set eventually compromises that separation.

items.label: Public timestamp
items.description: A public record of when the proposed analysis was specified.

items.label: Registered protocol
items.description: A timestamped protocol distinguishes planned analyses from later exploration. Exploration remains valuable, but it should not be relabeled as an earlier prediction.

items.label: Independent team
items.description: Another team with enough procedural detail to attempt the work in its own setting.

items.label: Replication protocol
items.description: An independent team receives enough detail to attempt the study. Independence is not sameness: differences in setting may reveal limits to the original claim.

items.label: Interpretable replication
items.description: The replication reports its uncertainty, allowing disagreement to be interpreted rather than reduced to a pass/fail slogan. A noisy replication may be inconclusive.

items.label: Robustness report
items.description: The report compares replication and held-out performance. Agreement is informative; unexplained disagreement becomes part of the record instead of disappearing into a success badge.

items.label: Resource map
items.description: The fictional canal system, including upstream and downstream connections.

items.label: User testimony
items.description: Accounts of water needs, including users missing from the official roster.

items.label: User-resource map
items.description: The map identifies upstream and downstream canal users, including people whose needs were absent from the official list. A resource boundary and a social boundary need not coincide.

items.label: Seasonal demand
items.description: Dry-season needs that exceed the available water in this illustrative case.

items.label: Allocation problem
items.description: Dry-season demand exceeds the water available in the fictional case. Naming the shortage prevents a rule from promising every user everything.

items.label: Local deliberation
items.description: A discussion in which affected users can propose and question allocation rules.

items.label: Allocation rule
items.description: Users propose a timed allocation rule. It is a candidate agreement shaped by local needs, not a universal optimum supplied by the game.

items.label: Observable indicators
items.description: Recorded flows or other outcomes that make a proposed rule's performance inspectable.

items.label: Monitoring agreement
items.description: Observable flows and turns make compliance discussable. Monitoring can still be costly or uneven, so a measurable rule is not automatically a fair one.

items.label: Accessible appeal
items.description: A route for an affected person to challenge a decision and have their reasons heard.

items.label: Accountable procedure
items.description: A user can contest a recorded violation through an accessible appeal. Accountability changes who can challenge enforcement; it does not guarantee every appeal succeeds.

items.label: Revision meeting
items.description: An agreed opportunity to revise a rule after experience exposes its limits.

items.label: Revisable charter
items.description: The charter specifies how users can revise the rule after a dry season. A durable institution can include a way to change rather than pretending initial foresight was perfect.

items.label: Neighboring authorities
items.description: Other groups with responsibilities beyond the local group's boundary.

items.label: Nested agreement
items.description: Neighboring authorities coordinate across boundaries that one canal group cannot govern alone. Ostrom's work motivates contextual, nested arrangements, not the claim that commons always beat states or markets.

items.label: Training examples
items.description: Recorded cases selected for fitting a predictor, not a complete representation of the world.

items.label: Learning rule
items.description: The specified procedure that fits patterns in the training examples.

items.label: Trained predictor
items.description: The predictor learns patterns from the supplied examples. It learns from a selection of recorded cases, not directly from every situation it may later encounter.

items.label: Validation result
items.description: Held-out cases estimate performance on data withheld from fitting. A good score here need not survive a different deployment population.

items.label: Deployment cases
items.description: Examples from the actual intended setting, which may differ from the training collection.

items.label: Generalization assessment
items.description: Deployment examples reveal where the new setting differs. Generalization is a question to investigate, not a property conferred by calling a model intelligent.

items.label: Subgroup errors
items.description: Errors examined separately across relevant groups instead of hidden inside one average.

items.label: Disaggregated evaluation
items.description: Errors are separated by relevant groups instead of hidden inside one average. Which groups and errors matter is partly a social decision, not just an arithmetic one.

items.label: Documented limits
items.description: Known uses or settings for which the available evaluation does not support a claim.

items.label: Model card
items.description: The model card records intended use, evaluation and known limits. It makes claims inspectable rather than guaranteeing trustworthiness by documentation alone.

items.label: Contestable decision process
items.description: A person affected by a decision can challenge the evidence or application. The process preserves human recourse instead of treating a prediction as an unanswerable judgment.

items.label: Outcome monitoring
items.description: Records of what happens after deployment, including challenges and unanticipated harms.

items.label: Audited service
items.description: Outcomes and appeals are reviewed after deployment. New harms or changed conditions can prompt restriction or withdrawal; an audit is ongoing work, not permanent certification.

items.label: Local astronomical time
items.description: The ship’s local time at the same instant as the lunar observation, inferred from an astronomical observation in this idealized example.

items.label: Gravity-law case study
items.description: A case sheet pairing a proposed inverse-square attraction with recorded orbital motion; not a consequence of mass times acceleration alone.

items.label: Woodblock
items.description: A surface that can carry a whole carved page and be retained for later impressions.

items.label: Carved edition
items.description: The fictional workshop carves the selected edition into a block. Its text and image can be retained together for later runs; revising that surface has a cost.

items.label: Paper and ink
items.description: The workshop's reusable printing supplies, abstracted as one material kit rather than finite inventory.

items.label: Woodblock print
items.description: Paper and ink take an impression from the prepared block. The result shows that a sophisticated printed page does not require movable type.

items.label: Movable type
items.description: Reusable character pieces that must be selected, arranged and stored by the workshop.

items.label: Typeset edition
items.description: Reusable pieces of type are assembled for the same edition. Setting and storing a character inventory is work, not an automatically superior replacement for carving.

items.label: Type print
items.description: The type produces another printed page. Similar visible results can hide very different preparation and revision workflows.

items.label: Unchanged reprint order
items.description: A fictional customer asks for another run of exactly the existing edition.

items.label: Stored-block advantage
items.description: For this unchanged reprint order, a preserved block avoids resetting the page. This local advantage does not prove block printing is always cheaper.

items.label: Revised edition order
items.description: A different fictional order changes passages before another run is printed.

items.label: Reset-type advantage
items.description: For this revised order, reusable type can be rearranged instead of recarving a whole page. The advantage depends on the revision, available type and workshop labor.

items.label: Workflow comparison
items.description: The two orders favor different workflows. Their coexistence challenges the simple story that one invention must immediately make the other obsolete.

items.label: Patronage records
items.description: Records of what patrons wanted, what they could fund and which workshops could undertake it.

items.label: Contextual adoption account
items.description: Patrons, editions, skills and available materials help explain adoption alongside technical possibilities. This fictional comparison illustrates a historical question; it does not establish one universal cause for East Asian printing choices.

items.label: Conflicting recollections
items.description: Two former residents give incompatible accounts of a fictional eviction; only one directly witnessed the decisive disputed act.

items.label: Competing reconstructions
items.description: In this fiction, two former residents remember incompatible eviction scenes; the dated street photograph constrains both but settles neither. The reconstruction now has alternatives instead of a single authoritative past.

items.label: Spatial reconstruction engine
items.description: A fictional system that renders walkable models from records; it cannot make missing evidence true.

items.label: Walkable neighborhood
items.description: The fictional spatial engine lets visitors walk the competing neighborhood models. The new power is vivid access to lost places; vividness can also make an uncertain account feel indisputably real.

items.label: Ownership claim
items.description: A present-day restitution claim whose support depends partly on the disputed reconstruction.

items.label: Disputed restitution
items.description: An ownership claimant uses the reconstructed scene to seek restitution. A compelling simulation now affects present rights, even though its evidential gaps have not vanished.

items.label: Withdrawn testimony
items.description: A contributor withdraws private testimony; its evidential absence must remain visible rather than silently regenerated.

items.label: Public court record
items.description: A surviving public record relevant to the disputed eviction, incomplete on its own.

items.label: Evidence-gap map
items.description: The only private witness to the decisive disputed act withdraws testimony, while a public court record survives; the other resident’s account of that act is indirect. The map marks what remains supported and what cannot be reconstructed from admissible material.

items.label: Uncertainty overlay
items.description: An overlay ties disputed parts of each scene to their sources and gaps. Visitors can see uncertainty rather than mistake a smooth rendering for complete knowledge.

items.label: Qualified reconstruction
items.description: The walkable reconstruction keeps those uncertainty marks visible. It gains honesty at the cost of a seamless illusion; the missing testimony is not magically recovered by consent software.

items.label: Appeal hearing
items.description: A forum for recording conflicting restitution claims, not an automatic mechanism for perfect justice.

items.label: Contested case file
items.description: The hearing records conflicting claims and reasons without making the player pronounce a final legal verdict. Procedural access does not erase unequal resources between claimants.

items.label: Open restitution case
items.description: The restitution case remains open beside a qualified reconstruction. Descendants gain a way to contest erasure, but the archive cannot manufacture the unknowable event that would settle every claim.

items.label: Mirror orbit
items.description: A fictional orbital-reflector proposal; its ability to provide useful crop lighting remains a model assumption.

items.label: Seasonal crop model
items.description: A fictional model relating the timing of extra light to growth, with other requirements still unresolved.

items.label: Extended-light forecast
items.description: In the fictional model, a mirror schedule adds light during part of the growing season. Extra light is only a proposed benefit: crops also depend on heat, water and biological responses.

items.label: Water budget
items.description: A finite water constraint that limits the promised harvest benefit in the speculative case.

items.label: Conditional harvest forecast
items.description: The water budget limits the modeled harvest gain. A brighter field is not automatically a larger sustainable harvest, and the forecast is explicitly conditional.

items.label: Night-sky survey
items.description: Records of darkness needed for a neighboring observatory's measurements.

items.label: Mirror schedule
items.description: The proposed timing of reflected illumination, which overlaps some dark-time activities.

items.label: Lost observing window
items.description: The schedule overlaps a neighboring observatory's dark-time window. The same reflected light is a resource for one group and lost observing capacity for another.

items.label: Nocturnal habitat record
items.description: Evidence about ecological uses of darkness that a crop-yield calculation leaves out.

items.label: Darkness-impact map
items.description: The habitat record expands the dispute beyond people and telescopes. Darkness has ecological roles that a simple crop-yield total would leave out.

items.label: Alternative orbit
items.description: A modeled alternative reducing reflected light and some benefits as well as some harms.

items.label: Lower-light plan
items.description: An alternative orbit reduces the illumination and the predicted crop benefit. This is a concrete compromise, not a discovery of a free solution that satisfies everyone.

items.label: Shared-sky proposal
items.description: The proposal displays harvest limits beside observing and habitat losses. Different communities can reasonably weigh those outcomes differently; the artifact makes the disagreement legible.

items.label: Shutter control
items.description: A fictional actuator that stops further reflection, not a time machine undoing prior effects.

items.label: Stoppable pilot
items.description: The fictional shutter can halt further illumination. Stoppable operation is a technical control, not proof that earlier ecological or social effects can be reversed.

items.label: Long-term effects register
items.description: A record separating immediate operation from ecological and social consequences that might persist.

items.label: Irreversible-risk record
items.description: The record separates what stops immediately from changes that may persist. It rejects the tempting equation 'off switch equals no lasting harm.'

items.label: Living atlas of consequences
items.description: The memory dispute and mirror dispute enter one atlas: new powers can illuminate lost places or dark fields while changing whose evidence, rights and environment count. The shared achievement is a contestable account of consequences, not unanimous progress.

locations.label: Dark room
locations.description: A room that excludes stray light so a small aperture can project an observable image.

locations.label: Trial ship
locations.description: A sea trial subjects a timekeeper to motion and changing conditions. A successful trial is evidence, not a guarantee for every voyage.

recipes.description: The notebook records where, when and how the observation was made. In this teaching case, two pots seem to dry at different rates; a memory of 'the drier one' would lose important context.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: Comparing the notes suggests that the sunnier pot dries sooner. A pattern gives us a question, not yet an explanation: the pots might also differ in size.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: One candidate explanation is that greater light exposure increases drying in this setup. It remains a hypothesis rather than a discovery about every plant or climate.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: If the proposed explanation matters, otherwise similar pots under different light should lose different amounts of water. That prediction makes a possible failure visible.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: A known reference exposes an offset in the scale. Calibration ties readings to a standard; it does not remove every source of error.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: Repeated readings reveal small fluctuations that a single reading would hide. Keep the variation rather than choosing the most pleasing number.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The record pairs each reading with its conditions. Another observer can now ask whether the difference is larger than the measurement uncertainty.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The teaching comparison changes light while holding pot size and starting water fixed. Controlling these conditions narrows the explanations; it does not guarantee all confounders vanished.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The written protocol says what will be compared, measured and recorded. It turns a private trick into a procedure another person can attempt.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The arrangement can be repeated from the record. A later attempt may disagree: repeatability is an opportunity to test the result, not a promise of agreement.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The speaker claims the new levy is fair because everyone pays the same amount. A reason is now visible, so an audience can challenge its relevance instead of merely disliking the conclusion.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The hidden premise is that equal amounts imply equal burdens. Naming it reveals where people who agree about the figures may still disagree.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: In this supplied example, 'all citizens covered by rule R must pay; this person is covered by R; therefore this person must pay' has a valid form. Validity does not establish that the rule or premises are just or true.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: One low-income household and one wealthy household can pay the same amount while bearing very different burdens. That counterexample defeats the universal equal-burden claim, not every possible argument for the levy.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The speakers have used 'equal' to mean both equal amounts and equal sacrifice. A shared word was concealing two different questions.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: Here 'equal amount' refers only to the numerical payment. The clarified term prevents one meaning being silently substituted for another.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The question becomes 'Which principle of fairness should determine the payment?' Clear wording exposes a genuine disagreement rather than automatically resolving it.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: The copies preserve different words in the same passage. Collation puts the alternatives beside one another without deciding that the oldest-looking copy must be right.
recipes.caveat: Conceptual teaching relationship, not a claim that these two inputs alone historically caused this development.

recipes.description: A quoted opening phrase—the lemma—identifies the passage being discussed. This reconstruction does not give ancient Alexandrian commentary modern line numbers.

recipes.description: A workshop problem becomes x + 5 = 12: the unknown is represented without guessing its value. The equality states a constraint, not a magic answer.

recipes.description: Subtracting 5 from both sides preserves this equality, leaving x = 7. Applying an operation on only one side would change the problem.

recipes.description: Completing the square turns a quadratic into a form from which candidate roots can be checked. The algebraic method extends the geometric example; domain and sign conditions still matter.
